title: New shortness of breath, post-op
objectives: Recognize and respond to a change in condition with a full assessment
Escalate to the provider using SBAR with the right findings
Write a change-of-condition note that documents findings, not a diagnosis

patient.name: Maria Alvarez
medications: Oxycodone 5 mg PO q4h PRN pain

opening: It's 1400 and you're passing through for hourly rounding. Mrs. Alvarez says she 'just doesn't feel right' and is more short of breath than she was at breakfast. She's sitting up in bed, looks pale, and is breathing faster than normal. Her surgical dressing is intact. Nothing about this was in report.

actions.label: Take a full set of vitals
actions.detail: Including pulse ox and respiratory rate — don't rely on what's already on the board.
actions.response: BP 110/64, HR 118, RR 26, Temp 101.6, SpO2 90% on room air. Pain unchanged at 4/10.

actions.label: Auscultate lung sounds
actions.detail: She says she's short of breath — listen before assuming why.
actions.response: Diminished breath sounds at the right base, no wheeze or stridor. Mild accessory muscle use. No jugular venous distension.
actions.criticalWhy: Post-op patients are at risk for atelectasis, pneumonia, and PE — a focused lung exam narrows what you're escalating about.

actions.label: Inspect the surgical site
actions.detail: Rule out a surgical source before assuming this is pulmonary.
actions.response: Dressing clean, dry, and intact. No erythema, drainage, or increased tenderness at the incision.

actions.label: Check capillary blood glucose
actions.detail: She's diabetic and her metformin is held — rule out a metabolic cause too.
actions.response: Fingerstick glucose 142 mg/dL. Not the driver here, but now you can rule it out when you call.

actions.label: Notify the provider using SBAR
actions.detail: Situation, background, assessment, recommendation — with the numbers in front of you.
actions.response: You reach Dr. Nguyen and report the vitals, lung findings, and clear surgical site. New orders: STAT portable chest X-ray, blood cultures x2, start supplemental O2 at 2L NC, repeat vitals q30min.

actions.label: Apply supplemental oxygen and recheck SpO2
actions.detail: Per the new order — 2L nasal cannula.
actions.response: SpO2 improves to 95% on 2L NC. She reports feeling a little easier to breathe.

actions.label: Give her PRN oxycodone for the pain first
actions.detail: She's uncomfortable and it's an easy fix.
actions.response: Pain isn't what she's reporting — she's short of breath. Treating the wrong problem delays finding the real one, and opioids can blunt respiratory drive in a patient who may already be hypoxic.

actions.label: Reassure her it's probably just anxiety
actions.response: New tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia in a post-op patient are not anxiety until everything else has been ruled out. Assuming a benign cause without assessing first can miss a PE, pneumonia, or sepsis.

actions.label: Call her family to let them know she seems unwell
actions.response: Family notification matters, but not before the patient is assessed and the provider is notified. Stabilize and escalate first.

actions.label: Chart that she is developing pneumonia
actions.detail: The lung findings point that way.
actions.response: Diagnosing is the provider's job, not yours. Charting a diagnosis you're not authorized to make — even one that turns out to be right — is a documentation error. Chart what you found: the vitals, the lung sounds, what you did.

hints: She's diabetic, post-op, and suddenly short of breath — what's the fastest way to know how worried to be?
Rule out the obvious sources — the wound, the lungs, the blood sugar — before you call.
SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation. Have your numbers ready before you dial.

documentation.placeholder: Begin with the time and what you noticed...

requirements.label: What you noticed and when
requirements.why: Anchors the note in time and shows you responded promptly to a subjective complaint, not just a monitor alarm.

requirements.label: No diagnosis you're not authorized to make
requirements.why: Diagnosing is outside your scope. A guess in the note becomes a claim in the record.

requirements.label: Full vital signs, including SpO2 and respiratory rate
requirements.why: These numbers are the objective evidence that something changed.

requirements.label: Lung assessment findings
requirements.why: Shows you did a focused assessment, not just took vitals.

requirements.label: Surgical site assessed and ruled out
requirements.why: Closes off one obvious differential and shows thoroughness.

requirements.label: Blood glucose checked
requirements.why: She's diabetic — ruling out a metabolic cause is expected.

requirements.label: Provider notified, with time and new orders
requirements.why: Times and names, and what changed as a result.

requirements.label: Oxygen therapy started and response documented
requirements.why: An intervention without a documented response is only half the story.

requirements.label: Plan for continued monitoring
requirements.why: Closes the loop: what happens next.

documentation.modelNote:
1400 — Resident reports subjective shortness of breath and 'not feeling right' during hourly rounding; appears pale, mild tachypnea noted on entry. VS: BP 110/64, HR 118, RR 26, SpO2 90% on room air, Temp 101.6, pain 4/10. Lung sounds diminished at right base, no wheeze or stridor, mild accessory muscle use, no JVD. Surgical site clean/dry/intact, no erythema or drainage. Fingerstick glucose 142.

1413 — Dr. Nguyen notified via SBAR of above findings. New orders received: STAT portable chest X-ray, blood cultures x2, oxygen 2L via nasal cannula, vitals q30min.

Oxygen applied at 2L via NC; SpO2 improved to 95%, resident reports easier breathing. Will continue frequent monitoring per new order and notify provider of any further change.
pitfalls: Writing 'patient seems anxious' as the explanation instead of documenting the objective findings.
Charting a diagnosis ('developing pneumonia') instead of the assessment that prompted the workup.
Leaving out the time the provider was reached, or the orders received.
Documenting that oxygen was started but not whether it helped.
